title: Most Probable Velocity of Gas Molecules
short_intro: The most probable velocity is the speed possessed by the maximum fraction of molecules in a gas at a given absolute temperature. It corresponds to the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann molecular speed distribution curve.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition, formula, dependence on temperature and molar mass, comparison with root-mean-square and average velocities.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation from Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution function, differentiation to find the maxima, and kinetic interpretation of temperature.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Origin
bullets: It is the velocity corresponding to the peak (maximum) of the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution curve.
Molecules of a gas possess a wide range of speeds due to continuous elastic collisions among themselves.
The number of molecules having the most probable velocity is greater than the number having any other specific velocity interval.

concept_notes.heading: Dependence on Temperature and Mass
bullets: Directly proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature of the gas (v<sub>mp</sub> ∝ √T).
Inversely proportional to the square root of the molecular mass or molar mass of the gas (v<sub>mp</sub> ∝ 1 / √M).
Independent of pressure at constant temperature for an ideal gas.

concept_notes.heading: Comparison of Molecular Speeds
bullets: The three characteristic speeds follow the fixed ratio: v<sub>mp</sub> : v<sub>avg</sub> : v<sub>rms</sub> = √(2RT/M) : √(8RT/πM) : √(3RT/M) = √2 : √(8/π) : √3 ≈ 1 : 1.128 : 1.224.
Root-mean-square velocity is always greater than average velocity, which in turn is greater than most probable velocity (v<sub>rms</sub> > v<sub>avg</sub> > v<sub>mp</sub>).
This ordering reflects the asymmetry of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve.

concept_notes.heading: Role in Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
bullets: Obtained mathematically by setting the first derivative of the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution function with respect to speed equal to zero.
Represents the most frequent outcome of random thermal motion in macroscopic thermodynamic equilibrium.
Shifts to higher values as thermal energy increases.

derivations.title: Derivation of Most Probable Velocity from Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
steps: Start with the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution function: dN<sub>v</sub> / N = 4π (m / 2πkT)<sup>3/2</sup> v<sup>2</sup> exp(-mv<sup>2</sup> / 2kT) dv.
To find the peak of the distribution, differentiate the function with respect to v and set the derivative equal to zero: d/dv [v<sup>2</sup> exp(-mv<sup>2</sup> / 2kT)] = 0.
Apply the product rule of differentiation: 2v exp(-mv<sup>2</sup> / 2kT) + v<sup>2</sup> (-mv / kT) exp(-mv<sup>2</sup> / 2kT) = 0.
Factor out common terms: v exp(-mv<sup>2</sup> / 2kT) [2 - (mv<sup>2</sup> / kT)] = 0.
Since v ≠ 0 at the peak and exponential term is non-zero, equate the bracketed term to zero: 2 - (mv<sup>2</sup> / kT) = 0.
Solve for v to get the most probable velocity: v<sub>mp</sub> = √(2kT / m) = √(2RT / M).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Maxwell-Boltzmann Speed Distribution Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of fraction of molecules (dN/dv) on the y-axis against molecular speed (v) on the x-axis, showing an asymmetric bell-shaped curve skewed to the right.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The peak of the curve corresponds to v_mp. The area under the curve represents the total number of molecules. v_avg and v_rms lie to the right of v_mp due to the long tail.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in identifying positions of v_mp, v_avg, and v_rms on the curve, and effect of temperature change.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effect of Temperature on Distribution Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two curves at temperatures T_1 and T_2 (where T_2 > T_1). The higher temperature curve is flatter, broader, and its peak shifts to the right and downward.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As temperature increases, the most probable velocity increases, and the spread of molecular velocities becomes wider.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual questions regarding shifting of peaks and molecular speed changes at varying temperatures.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Molecular Speeds Comparison Bar/Visual representation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Relative positions of v_mp, v_avg, and v_rms marked on a common velocity axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Clearly depicts that v_mp < v_avg < v_rms always for any ideal gas.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct ordering and ratio MCQ questions in TGT/PGT examinations.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the most probable velocity of oxygen molecules (M = 32 g/mol) at 27 °C. Given R = 8.314 J/mol K.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: T = 27 °C = 300 K, M = 32 g/mol = 32 × 10<sup>-3</sup> kg/mol, R = 8.314 J/mol K.

solved_numericals.question: At what temperature will the most probable velocity of hydrogen molecules (M = 2 g/mol) be equal to the root-mean-square velocity of oxygen molecules (M = 32 g/mol) at 300 K?
solution_steps: Find v_rms of oxygen at 300 K: v_rms(O2) = √(3 R T_O2 / M_O2) = √(3 R × 300 / 32).
Equate to v_mp of hydrogen at unknown temperature T: v_mp(H2) = √(2 R T / M_H2) = √(2 R T / 2) = √(RT).
Cancel R and solve for T: T = 900 / 32 = 28.125 K.

solved_numericals.question: If the absolute temperature of an ideal gas is increased four times, by what factor does the most probable velocity of its molecules increase?
solution_steps: Express initial and final states: v_mp1 = K √T_1 and v_mp2 = K √T_2.
Take the ratio: v_mp2 / v_mp1 = √(T_2 / T_1) = √(4 T_1 / T_1) = √4 = 2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the gas obeys the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution law, which strictly holds only for ideal gases in thermal equilibrium at low densities.
Fails at extremely high pressures and low temperatures where intermolecular quantum effects and real gas van der Waals interactions become significant.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Most probable velocity is equal to the average velocity of gas molecules.
common_misconceptions.correct: Most probable velocity is less than the average velocity (v_mp < v_avg).
common_misconceptions.why: The distribution curve is asymmetric (skewed to the right), which shifts the arithmetic mean and root-mean-square values to higher speeds than the peak.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Most probable velocity depends on the pressure of the gas.
common_misconceptions.correct: Most probable velocity depends only on temperature and molar mass (v_mp = √(2RT/M)).
common_misconceptions.why: Pressure changes alter density proportionally at constant temperature, keeping the ratio P/ρ constant for an ideal gas.
